name: Water loading / hydration maxxing
summary: Drinking large amounts of water for skin and depuffing: fixed targets like eight glasses lack scientific basis, and excess carries hyponatremia risk.
lead: Water loading, sometimes called hydration maxxing, is the practice of deliberately drinking large quantities of water in the belief that it improves skin or reduces puffiness.

name: 16:8 time-restricted eating
summary: Eat inside an eight-hour window and fast the other sixteen; the research is about weight and metabolic markers, not looks.
lead: 16:8 time-restricted eating (TRE) is a daily meal-timing pattern in which all food is eaten within an eight-hour window, leaving sixteen hours of fasting, often overnight plus part of the morning and evening. It belongs to the family of time-restricted eating, in which food is confined to a set daily window, commonly 8 to 12 hours.

name: Alternate-day fasting
summary: Fast every other day; trials show weight loss, but not clearly more than ordinary calorie cutting.
lead: Alternate-day fasting (ADF) is an intermittent fasting pattern in which fast days alternate with unrestricted "feast" days. In the strict form no calories are eaten on fast days; in the modified form roughly a quarter of usual energy needs, often 0 to 500 kcal, is allowed.

name: 5:2 diet
summary: Eat normally five days, eat about 500 calories on two; weight loss is similar to ordinary dieting.
lead: The 5:2 diet is an intermittent fasting pattern in which people eat normally for five days a week and limit intake to roughly 500 to 600 calories on two non-consecutive days. It was popularised in the UK and Australia by Michael Mosley after a 2012 BBC documentary.

name: Fasting-mimicking diet
summary: A five-day low-calorie cycle from Valter Longo; studied for aging markers and disease, not for looks.
lead: The fasting-mimicking diet (FMD) is a five-day, low-calorie, low-protein, plant-based eating cycle designed to reproduce some physiological effects of water fasting while still supplying limited food. It was developed by biogerontologist Valter Longo at the University of Southern California.

name: Dry fasting
summary: No food and no water; research covers religious daytime fasts, while longer dry fasts carry dehydration risk.
lead: Dry fasting is abstaining from both food and fluids for a period of time. It occurs in religious practice, such as daytime fasts of the Bahá'í Faith and Ramadan, and in some wellness circles that advocate longer dry fasts.

name: Bulking
summary: Eat above maintenance to build muscle; the debate is how much fat comes along.
lead: Bulking is a planned phase of eating above maintenance calories, combined with resistance training, to gain muscle and body weight. It is the counterpart of cutting, in which fat is lost.
claims: A calorie surplus is the way to gain muscle.
Natural lifters do not need to bulk beyond early training.
A small surplus of about 250 calories gives minimal fat gain.

name: Dirty bulk
summary: Eating a large, loosely tracked calorie surplus to gain weight fast; quick scale gains, more fat to cut later.
lead: A dirty bulk is a bulking strategy in which a person eats a large calorie surplus without carefully tracking macronutrients or food quality, often relying on calorie-dense foods such as burgers and fries. It is contrasted with a clean bulk, which uses a smaller surplus and more controlled food choices to limit fat gain.
claims: Clean bulking is better than dirty bulking for looks
Dirty bulking suits people using steroids

name: Lean bulk
summary: A small calorie surplus aimed at adding muscle while limiting fat gain; slower than a dirty bulk.
lead: A lean bulk, also called a clean bulk or lean gaining, is a muscle-building phase that uses a small calorie surplus and resistance training to gain muscle while limiting fat gain. It takes longer than a large-surplus approach but is described as more precise.
claims: A small surplus (around 500 kcal) lets you add muscle without getting fat
Natural lifters are stuck choosing between looking skinny and looking soft

name: Cutting
summary: A calorie-deficit phase to lose fat and show muscle and bone definition; a staple of looksmaxxing leanness advice.
lead: Cutting is a phase of eating in a net negative energy balance, a calorie deficit, to lose body fat while preserving as much muscle as possible. In competitive bodybuilding, athletes typically spend an off-season building muscle and then cut for roughly 12 to 14 weeks before a contest.
claims: Cutting during puberty can stunt growth or cost height and bone mass
Dropping to low body fat noticeably improves appearance
Aggressive deficits cause muscle loss and hormonal effects

name: Leanmaxxing
summary: Losing body fat to show facial bone structure and a sharper jawline; the most common first step in looksmaxxing.
lead: Leanmaxxing is a looksmaxxing term for lowering body fat, with the aim of revealing facial bone structure and a leaner overall look. It is discussed on looksmax.org through many threads, including motivational posts, tips, guides and progress updates.
claims: Lower body fat makes the face more defined and attractive
Getting below about 15 percent body fat is especially difficult
Drugs such as GLP-1 agonists help leanmaxxing

name: Recomp
summary: Body recomposition: losing fat and gaining muscle at the same time, mostly discussed for beginners and skinny-fat lifters.
lead: Recomp, short for body recomposition, is the attempt to reduce body fat and build muscle at the same time, in contrast with alternating a bulk and a cut. It is discussed on looksmaxxing forums mainly in relation to skinny-fat bodies, where a person has low muscle and relatively high fat.
claims: Skinny-fat people should not recomp and should bulk or cut instead
Drugs plus L-carnitine allow recomp even while bulking
A small daily deficit with high protein can lose fat while keeping muscle

name: Mini-cut
summary: A short, aggressive calorie deficit used to drop a few pounds of fat quickly, often between bulks.
lead: A mini-cut is a short, aggressive cutting phase in which a lifter eats well below maintenance for a few weeks to reduce body fat, usually between longer bulking phases. A Grokipedia summary describes them as lasting about 2 to 6 weeks.

name: Calorie counting
summary: Logging every kilocalorie to cut or bulk; the standard tool for leanness, with eating-disorder caveats.
lead: Calorie counting is the practice of logging the energy content of everything eaten, usually in kilocalories and often with a phone app or food scale, in order to hold intake above or below a target. In looksmaxxing communities it is mainly used for fat loss ("cutting") to reveal facial and body leanness, and in reverse for deliberate weight gain.
claims: Tracking calories precisely is the most reliable route to a leaner face.
Counting is unnecessary because meal timing alone can produce loss.
Constant tracking can become unhealthy for some people.

name: Macro tracking / IIFYM
summary: Tracking grams of protein, carbs and fat instead of just calories; common in cutting and bulking, little direct research.
lead: Macro tracking is the practice of logging daily grams of protein, carbohydrate and fat, rather than only total calories. "If It Fits Your Macros" (IIFYM) is the label for a flexible version in which any food is acceptable provided the targets are met. In looksmaxxing and fitness communities it is used to drive fat loss or muscle gain.

name: Protein shakes / whey
summary: Milk-derived powder for hitting protein targets; about as effective as other protein sources, with no facial-appearance studies.
lead: Whey protein is a mixture of proteins isolated from whey, the liquid left when milk is curdled for cheese, and is sold as a powder for protein shakes. It is mainly used to meet protein targets for muscle building and recovery, which looksmaxxing communities link to body composition and a leaner, more muscular frame.

name: Gallon of milk a day (GOMAD)
summary: A gallon of whole milk a day for a big calorie surplus; popular in strength circles, untested as a named method.
lead: GOMAD, short for "gallon of milk a day", is a weight-gain method from strength-training communities in which a lifter drinks roughly a gallon of whole milk daily on top of regular meals to create a large calorie surplus. Looksmaxxing spaces discuss it as a way to add mass.

name: Big dirty bulk (Fast-food bulking)
summary: Eating a huge surplus of junk food to gain mass fast; faster gains reported, but more fat to cut afterward.
lead: A dirty bulk is a weight-gain approach in which a person eats a large calorie surplus without carefully tracking macronutrients, often using calorie-dense convenience or fast food. It contrasts with a "clean bulk" that aims to gain muscle with little fat.

name: Eating for jaw (chewing hard foods)
summary: Chewing tough foods to grow the masseter; the muscle can enlarge with heavy chewing, but hard-food diets are untested.
lead: Eating for jaw is the practice of regularly chewing tough or hard foods in the hope of enlarging the masseter and sharpening the jawline. It is discussed in looksmaxxing communities alongside mastic gum and jaw exercisers.

name: Low-carb to lose face puffiness
summary: Cutting carbs to drop glycogen-bound water and look leaner in the face; the water shift is well described, face-specific results are untested.
lead: Using a low-carbohydrate diet to reduce facial puffiness is a practice discussed in looksmaxxing and physique communities in which people restrict carbohydrates, sometimes briefly before a photo or event, in the belief that this reduces water retention and sharpens facial features. It is usually framed as a short-term appearance tactic rather than a long-term diet.
claims: Cutting carbs makes the face look leaner within days.
Low-carb eating reduces facial fat specifically.
Short low-carb stints are harmless.

name: Carb cycling
summary: Alternating high- and low-carb days around training; popular with physique athletes, with little direct trial evidence.
lead: Carb cycling, or carbohydrate cycling, is a dietary approach that alternates days or longer periods of higher carbohydrate intake with lower-carbohydrate periods, commonly scheduling the high-carbohydrate days around intense training . Followers use it for fat loss, retaining muscle and training performance.
claims: Carb cycling burns more fat than steady dieting.
High-carb days refill glycogen and improve training.
Cycling prevents metabolic slowdown by resetting leptin.

name: Refeed days / diet breaks
summary: Planned higher-calorie days or weeks during a cut; popular in physique circles, thinly sourced here.
lead: Refeed days and diet breaks are planned periods of higher energy intake, commonly of extra carbohydrate, within a longer calorie-restricted diet. A refeed usually lasts a day or two, while a diet break lasts longer, such as a week at maintenance intake. They are discussed in bodybuilding and appearance-focused dieting communities.
claims: Refeeds make the physique look fuller.
Refeeds restart fat loss or prevent metabolic slowdown.

name: Sodium/potassium manipulation (peak week)
summary: Bodybuilder-style salt and water adjustments before a show or shoot; documented as part of contest prep, with associated health risks.
lead: Sodium and potassium manipulation during peak week refers to deliberate changes to salt, potassium and fluid intake in the days before a bodybuilding contest or photo shoot, with the stated aim of a drier, more defined look. It is part of the final contest-prep stage, which reference sources describe as combining carbohydrate loading with dehydration .
claims: Manipulating salt and water makes you look drier and more defined.
These methods are safe if done briefly.

name: Water cutting / dehydration pre-photo
summary: Restricting fluids to look drier or sharper for a photo; dehydration has well-documented health risks.
lead: Water cutting, or pre-photo dehydration, is the practice of intentionally limiting fluid intake in the hours or days before a photograph, contest or weigh-in in order to look drier or more defined. It is described as part of the final stage of bodybuilding contest preparation, which combines carbohydrate loading with dehydration .
claims: Dehydrating makes you look sharper in photos.
A short water cut has no meaningful downside.

name: Whole-food / unprocessed diet
summary: Cutting ultra-processed food in favour of minimally processed eating; observational links to health outcomes, no appearance trials.
lead: A whole-food or unprocessed diet emphasises foods in minimally processed form and limits ultra-processed foods (UPFs), a category defined by the NOVA classification proposed by Carlos Monteiro and colleagues at the University of São Paulo in 2009 and 2010 . In looksmaxxing communities it is promoted for general health, leanness and skin or face appearance.
claims: Cutting ultra-processed food improves skin and reduces facial bloating.
Ultra-processed food drives weight gain.

name: Clean eating
summary: A whole-foods eating style (the chicken, rice and broccoli staple) that forums link to clearer skin and leaner looks; research on its health effects is limited and has flagged links to disordered eating.
lead: Clean eating is an umbrella term for diets based on the belief that whole, unrefined foods bring health benefits and that processed or convenience foods should be avoided; some versions also exclude gluten, grains or dairy . The term is described as emerging in 1990s bodybuilding, where it meant high-protein, low-carbohydrate eating that avoided sugar and junk food in order to build lean muscle, and as broadening in the 2000s through a series of "Eat-Clean" books by Tosca Reno and later wellness bloggers and influencers .
claims: Eating clean improves skin and acne
A very clean diet makes the body more sensitive to insulin and androgen spikes
Clean-eating food is more nutritious than other food
Clean eating is a safe, flexible lifestyle rather than a diet

name: Eat the rainbow / skin nutrient diet
summary: Eating many colours of produce for antioxidants in hope of better skin; antioxidant supplements have shown no benefit or small harms in trials, and no skin studies of the colour approach were found.
lead: Eating the rainbow refers to eating produce in a variety of colours for the range of nutrients and pigments they contain. Wikipedia describes fruits and vegetables as good sources of vitamins C and E and of carotenoids, noting cooking can destroy some vitamins while raising the availability of some carotenoids .
claims: Antioxidant-rich produce improves skin

name: Oatmeal / fibre for gut-skin axis
summary: Eating oats and other fibre to feed gut bacteria in hope of clearer skin; fibre has documented gut and cholesterol effects, but skin benefits are untested in the sources reviewed.
lead: Dietary fibre is the portion of plant food not fully broken down by human digestive enzymes, including cellulose, resistant starch and pectins . Oats and barley contain beta-glucan, a soluble viscous fermentable fibre that has been shown to lower LDL cholesterol with regular intake .
claims: Oatmeal and fibre improve skin by improving gut health

name: Probiotics / fermented food for skin
summary: Probiotic supplements and fermented foods such as kefir and kimchi, used in hopes of clearer skin; acne research is described as preliminary.
lead: Probiotics are live microorganisms defined by the WHO in 2001 as conferring a health benefit on the host when administered in adequate amounts; the European Food Safety Authority rejects that definition because it builds in an unmeasurable health claim . Fermented foods such as yogurt, kefir, kimchi, sauerkraut and kombucha contain live cultures and have been eaten for centuries .
claims: Probiotics, kefir or kimchi can clear acne
Probiotics help eczema

name: Gut health protocols (gut-skin axis)
summary: Combined elimination and probiotic routines aimed at clearer skin via the gut; the underlying gut-skin links are mostly associations, and no trials of the bundled protocols were found.
lead: Gut health protocols for skin typically bundle elimination of suspected trigger foods with probiotics, fermented foods and fibre. The shared premise is a gut-skin axis in which gut microbes influence skin through immune and metabolic signalling.
claims: Fixing the gut clears the skin
